solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Furniture component well attached to lower surface

indicators.note: puts the well after the lower surface, joining the two pieces

parts.note: a bed is the lowest surface, as in a sea bed or river bed
a spring is a natural well, where water rises

explanation.surface: A description from a furniture catalogue of a part fixed to the underside of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like an adverb, as in 'well attached', and it is the noun: a source of water. 'Lower surface' reads as the underside of the furniture, and it is a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedspring is one of the coiled springs inside a bed or mattress, a component of a piece of furniture.

clue.text: Inferior shelters engineers exposed

indicators.note: to shelter something is to hold it inside

parts.note: inferior = bad, poor in quality
RE = Royal Engineers, the British Army corps

explanation.surface: Poor-quality shelters built by army engineers are left open to the elements.
explanation.walkthrough: RE for the Royal Engineers is a standard crossword abbreviation. BAD opens around it: BA + RE + D.
explanation.definitionFit: Bared means uncovered, laid open to view, which is exposed.

clue.text: Not totally evident a lass is tantalising healthcare worker

indicators.note: the answer is not all of the words, just a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the run starts after EVI in 'evident' and stops before ALISING in 'tantalising'

explanation.surface: Someone half-noticing a flirtatious young woman who happens to work in a clinic.
explanation.walkthrough: A fifteen-letter hidden answer is rare, which is why it hides so well; the run starts inside 'evident' and stops inside 'tantalising'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental assistant works alongside a dentist, so is a healthcare worker.

clue.text: Splendid taking up tour of chambers overlooking river

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking a word up turns it to read bottom to top
to overlook something is to leave it out, so R drops from ATRIAL

parts.note: a lap is a tour of a circuit; taken up, it reads PAL
ATRIAL (of atria, chambers of the heart) with R for river left out

explanation.surface: Someone admiring a guided tour of grand rooms that look out over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooking river' paints a view from a window, and it means ignoring the R. 'Of chambers' is the adjective ATRIAL, since atria are heart chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: Palatial means like a palace, splendid and grand.

clue.text: Where circus acts perform bounds of lunacy with determination

parts.note: circus acts perform in a tent, the big top

indicators.note: the bounds of a word are its edges, its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of LunacY

explanation.surface: A description of circus performers going at their mad stunts with total commitment.
explanation.walkthrough: The circus clause is a cryptic description that gives two words, IN TENT, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something intently is to do it with fixed purpose and determination.

clue.text: Happen to stop working

definitions.meaning: slang: 'what's going down?' means what is happening
a computer system goes down when it fails

explanation.surface: An instruction or a worry that a machine might just pack up by chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happen to' reads as one phrase, 'chance to', and the split falls after 'Happen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday: events go down, and servers go down.

clue.text: Revolutionary way figure presents

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the pieces read backwards

parts.note: St = street, a way
fig. = figure, as in a textbook caption

explanation.surface: A radical new way of presenting numbers or a diagram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presents' sits at the end looking like a verb, as if a figure were presenting something, and it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: presents here is the noun, things given, not the verb.

clue.text: Turning fat, short skinny monkey

definitions.note: a gibbon is strictly an ape, not a monkey; the clue uses the loose everyday sense

indicators.note: turning a word round makes it read backwards
a short word is missing its last letter

parts.note: BIG (fat) turned round
BONY (skinny) cut short, losing its Y

explanation.surface: A monkey that was plump becoming thin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' and 'skinny' look like a contradiction the surface is describing; each is simply a piece of wordplay, one reversed and one shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: The gibbon is a long-armed tree-swinging primate, loosely called a monkey.

clue.text: Breaking down feelings with Capitol riots

indicators.note: a riot is disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone emotionally overwhelmed by news of the riot at the US Capitol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the two fodder words, and 'riots' at the end stirs all fifteen letters. The Capitol is the US Congress building in Washington.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone falling to pieces is breaking down, losing control.

clue.text: Tattered rag's first of many torn using physical force

indicators.note: something tattered is torn to shreds, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: takes only the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the first letter of Many
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An old rag, ripped apart by many hands, is torn by brute force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Torn' looks like a second anagram indicator, echoing 'Tattered', and it is fodder: its letters go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong-arm describes tactics that rely on force or threats.

clue.text: Call telephone number about lock

indicators.note: turns the telephone abbreviation about, so it reads backwards

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them
TEL., the abbreviation seen before a telephone number, turned about

explanation.surface: Phoning a locksmith about a door lock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' is not the door kind but a lock of hair. TEL. is the abbreviation printed in front of a phone number.
explanation.definitionFit: Lock is taken in its hair sense, and the answer names one curled strand of that kind.

clue.text: Amateur mural ultimately delineated with felt-tip pen

indicators.note: takes the ultimate, or last, letter

parts.note: a dabber is a felt-tip marker, as used to mark bingo cards

indicators.note: to delineate is to outline

parts.note: the last letter of muraL

explanation.surface: A hobbyist painting a mural and finishing its outline with a marker pen.
explanation.walkthrough: The L sits in the middle of the pen. A dabber, or dauber, is the chunky felt-tip used to mark numbers at bingo, a British sense many solvers will not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A dabbler takes up something casually, without professional commitment: an amateur.

clue.text: Discussed current plan

indicators.note: what is discussed is spoken, so the word is said rather than spelt

parts.note: a draught is a current of air

explanation.surface: A meeting talking over the plan now in force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' reads as an adjective, present, and it is a noun: a draught of air. DRAUGHT is the British spelling; DRAFT sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a rough first version of a scheme or document is also its plan.

clue.text: Scientist's novel shocked nation

indicators.note: shocked hair stands every which way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: novel = new
NATION rearranged

explanation.surface: A scientist writes a novel that scandalises the whole country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, and it is the adjective NEW. The definition is the possessive 'Scientist’s', meaning belonging to Newton, the scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: Newtonian means of or belonging to Isaac Newton, the scientist.

clue.text: Scraps publicity charges for boring items

indicators.note: to charge something is to load it

parts.note: scraps = fights, brawls
an ad is publicity

explanation.surface: A company cutting its advertising fees for dull products.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scraps' looks like a verb, discards, and it is the noun: fights. 'Boring' reads as dull, and it means drilling holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A bradawl is a small pointed tool for boring holes in wood.

clue.text: Discuss speed on a cycle

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: bat = speed, as in 'going at a fair bat'
as written
a round is a cycle, as of events or duties

explanation.surface: Talking things over while riding fast on a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' looks like a bicycle, and it is a round. 'At a great bat' is British slang for at high speed.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: tossing an idea back and forth like a ball is a way to discuss it.

clue.text: Asian city a German visited regularly

indicators.note: calling at letters at regular intervals picks out every other one

parts.note: as written
the odd letters of GeRmAn

explanation.surface: A German tourist who keeps going back to an Asian city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says the German visited the city; in the wordplay the German is the word visited, letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Agra is the city in India that is home to the Taj Mahal.

clue.text: Dispirited and fed up with tardy daughter

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: FED written upwards
tardy = late
d = daughter, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A parent sick of a daughter who is always late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' reads as the idiom, sick of, and it splits: FED with 'up' as the instruction to reverse it.
explanation.definitionFit: Deflated means having lost confidence or spirit.

clue.text: Thoroughly investigates lodgings of Parisian with record

parts.note: digs is British slang for rented lodgings
de is French for 'of'
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A detective looking into a Parisian's rented rooms and his criminal record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of Parisian' means the word for 'of' in French, DE, not something belonging to a Parisian.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig deep is to investigate thoroughly, going beyond the surface.

clue.text: Shy to caress, releasing anxiety

indicators.note: to release something is to let it go, so CARE leaves CARESS

parts.note: as written
CARESS letting go of CARE (anxiety)

explanation.surface: A timid person reluctant to be touched, until the nerves melt away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' looks like the adjective, timid, and it is the verb: to throw, as at a coconut shy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shy is the verb meaning to throw, the sense kept in 'coconut shy', a fairground stall.

clue.text: Live in backward sleepy area somewhere in Spain

indicators.note: reads the word the wrong way round

parts.note: to be is to live, exist
IN reversed
a dorm (dormitory) is where people sleep

explanation.surface: Settling down in a sleepy, behind-the-times corner of Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backward' reads as describing a sleepy rural backwater, and it only turns IN round. Benidorm is a busy Spanish seaside resort, anything but sleepy.
explanation.definitionFit: Benidorm is a resort town on Spain's Costa Blanca.

clue.text: Cross top of range by climbing concealed nets

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter
in a down clue, climbing means read upwards
to net something is to catch it inside

parts.note: concealed = hid
R (top of Range) + BY, written upwards

explanation.surface: An angry climber crossing a summit and finding hidden nets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry or a verb, and it is the noun: a crossbreed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid is the offspring of a cross between two species or varieties.

clue.text: Look chestnut horse over

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the pieces read backwards

parts.note: chestnut is a reddish-brown colour
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A request to examine a chestnut horse.
explanation.walkthrough: RED + NAG turned over gives GANDER. 'Chestnut' is a horse's coat colour, which is why the surface reads so naturally. 'Take a gander' is British slang for have a look.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: 'take a gander' means have a look, so the noun stands for a glance.

clue.text: Lacking practice, fix cocktail

parts.note: a skill gets rusty without practice
to nail something is to fix it in place

explanation.surface: Someone out of practice trying to make a mixed drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A rusty nail is a cocktail of Scotch whisky and Drambuie.
explanation.definitionFit: The rusty nail is a well-known whisky cocktail.

clue.text: Sketch encapsulates back of designer garment

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose

parts.note: a skit is a short comic sketch

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of designeR

explanation.surface: A fashion drawing that shows the back view of a designer outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sketch' belongs with the designer in the surface, as a fashion drawing, and it is a comic skit.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is one kind of garment, worn from the waist down.

clue.text: River split after type of junction

indicators.note: 'after' in an across or down clue means placed later in reading order

parts.note: a T-junction, where one road meets another at right angles
a rent is a split or tear

explanation.surface: A river dividing where the roads meet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trent is a major river in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trent is one of England's longest rivers.

clue.text: Following cut, Freudian slips not broadcast

indicators.note: F, following, is cut from the word
a slip is a mistake, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: FREUDIAN with F (following) cut

explanation.surface: After a scandal, a presenter's Freudian slips never make it on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freudian slips' is one phrase in the surface; here 'slips' is the anagram signal. F for following is a standard abbreviation, as in 'p. 3 f.'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a programme never put on air has not been broadcast.

clue.text: Foodstuff from plant covering lake roughly to the west

indicators.note: in an across clue west is leftward, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a tree is a plant
L (lake) + CA (circa, roughly) written leftwards

explanation.surface: A food produced by a plant growing round a lake, somewhere westward.
explanation.walkthrough: CA, short for circa, means roughly. Treacle is the British name for molasses or golden syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacle is a syrup from sugar refining, a foodstuff.

clue.text: Old obsolete Tesla parts returned

indicators.note: the result is sent back, reading right to left

parts.note: obsolete = dead, no longer in use
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: An old Tesla car, its outdated parts sent back to the maker.
explanation.walkthrough: DE + T + AD makes DETAD, which reads DATED backwards. 'Parts' looks like car components, and it is a verb: T parts DEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated means old-fashioned, belonging to an earlier time.

clue.text: Set period to tidy up place again

indicators.note: to tidy up is to rearrange, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A fixed time slot allotted for tidying a place up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set period' reads as a fixed time, and its nine letters are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To redeposit something is to place or lay it down again.
